title: The idols and the axe
hook: Ibrahim breaks his people's idols and leaves the biggest one standing with the axe (21:57–58)

segments.voice: Yesterday: star, moon and sun, and Ibrahim's test, does it set? Today he takes that question indoors, to his own people's idols.

A row of carved figures in a temple, and a young man staring at them. Ibrahim asks his people why they worship them, and gets an answer you may have heard at home: that's how we've always done it. The Thanksgiving dish nobody actually likes. The route to Grandma's that takes twenty minutes longer. The way we just don't talk about Uncle Ray. It takes a certain kind of person to keep asking why after that. Usually a kid. And this time, Ibrahim doesn't stop at asking.
screen: `A ROW OF CARVED FIGURES.` → `THAT'S HOW WE'VE ALWAYS DONE IT.` → `A KID WHO KEEPS ASKING WHY.`

segments.voice: Surah twenty-one. Ibrahim says to his father and his people, in Pickthall's words: “What are these images unto which ye pay devotion?” Their answer, paraphrasing: we found our fathers worshipping them. That's the whole reason. Ibrahim says: then you and your fathers have been plainly wrong. And he makes a promise: by God, I'll deal with your idols once you've turned your backs and gone. The commentators say the whole town went out to a festival. While the temple stood empty, he broke the idols into pieces, in Pickthall's words, “all save the chief of them.” He left the biggest one standing, the verse says, so that they might turn to it. And the axe? The Qur'an never mentions one. It comes from the commentators' retelling, which says Ibrahim hung the axe on the big idol, or put it in its hand, as if to say: ask him. A vivid detail, and it's tradition, not the verse. What the verse does give is the trap: a room of smashed statues, and one big one left untouched. When the town comes back, they'll have to decide what they believe that big one can do. Ibrahim hasn't made a speech. He's made a question they can't avoid. Sometimes the kindest way to break a habit isn't to argue about it. It's to let the habit answer for itself.
screen: `WHAT ARE THESE IMAGES?` · `WE FOUND OUR FATHERS DOING IT.` · `ALL BROKEN BUT THE BIGGEST.` · `THE AXE COMES FROM TRADITION.` · then, large: `ALL SAVE THE CHIEF OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you do only because you've always done it. Hold it up the way Ibrahim looked at the row of images, and ask it plainly: why are you here, and what can you actually do? If you pray, ask for clear eyes.
Ibrahim. He broke his people's idols, left the biggest one standing, and let it wait for their questions.
Your line: ask the big one. Ibrahim left one idol standing so the question would stay in the room. Day thirty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 33 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "ASK THEM, IF THEY CAN SPEAK."`

howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Ibrahim and the idols to children as a lesson in thinking for oneself and in tawhid, and it's read in surahs twenty-one and thirty-seven.

original.note: Arabic: "a big one of theirs" (21:58), the idol Ibrahim left standing.

trapdoor: what you thought: Abraham smashed idols in anger.
what it means: the idols and the axe — Ibrahim breaks the images, leaves the biggest standing, and turns a habit into a question nobody can dodge.

what a scholar hears: 21:58 says he left the chief of them, that they might turn to it (or, some say, to him); the axe hung on the idol is from tafsir, not the Qur'an; the festival is in the commentators and in 37:88–93.

notes: Pickthall 21:52 and 21:58 quoted from memory (21:58: 'Then he reduced them to fragments, all save the chief of them, that haply they might have recourse unto it.'). Confirm.
The index title and hook mention the axe; the script keeps the title and says plainly the axe is from tafsir (al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir), not the Qur'an. A Keeper may want the index hook reworded.
'That they might turn to it': commentators differ whether the pronoun refers to the idol or to Ibrahim. The trapdoor mentions both.
The festival: from tafsir and 37:88–90 (he glanced at the stars and said 'I am sick'). Confirm.
'Uncle Ray' and Thanksgiving are American everyday examples; replace if preferred.
